events.text: The council gathers. Mission 1 begins.
Elena proposes Elena, Kenji. I know I am loyal, so I include myself to guarantee one Good member; with no role information yet, I choose Kenji as the second member.

I proposed Elena and Kenji. I know I am loyal, so including myself guarantees one Good member on the team. Kenji is not confirmed to me; with no role information, this is an initial probe. I ask everyone to evaluate this team on the information we have: there is no public evidence against Kenji yet, and rejecting without a concrete concern only delays mission 1. If anyone has a specific reason to doubt Kenji, state it; otherwise I favor approving this team and learning from the mission result.

I support this proposed team of Elena and myself. For transparency: I have no private information to share about anyone's alignment, and nothing in the game so far gives me a concrete reason to doubt any player. With a two-person team on Mission 1, the information landscape is simple: any successful mission here gives us a genuine signal, and a fail tells us at least one of the two members is Evil. I understand I am an unconfirmed pick, so let me offer what I can: I intend to play straightforwardly and openly, and I will be judging future proposals by the same standard I ask you to judge this one — concrete evidence, not vibes. Rejecting this team now would cost us a proposal and give us no new information, since no one has raised a specific concern about either member. Elena's reasoning is sound: she includes herself as a known-good baseline and takes a neutral second pick with no evidence against them. If anyone has an actual reason to doubt me or Elena, I welcome it being stated plainly — but absent that, approval and a mission result is the most informative path forward. I'll be voting to approve.

I'm supporting this team of Elena and Kenji. Mission 1 gives us very little information either way, and Elena's reasoning holds up: she includes herself as a known-good baseline, and nobody has raised a concrete concern about Kenji. Rejecting now would cost a proposal without telling us anything new. I'll approve it and judge the mission result as our first real data point. If anyone has specific evidence against either member, please state it now, before the vote.

I'm comfortable approving Elena and Kenji for Mission 1. Neither has given me reason to doubt them so far — Elena's self-inclusion as a baseline is standard and honest, and Kenji's transparency about having no private info is consistent with how a Loyal Servant would speak. Three of us have now voiced support, and no one has raised a concrete objection. I agree with the reasoning shared so far: rejecting this team without specific evidence just burns a proposal and delays our first real data point. Let's approve and see what the mission result tells us. Whatever comes back, we'll have our first piece of hard information to work with for Mission 2. I'm voting approve.

I agree with the consensus here. On Mission 1, Elena putting herself forward alongside Kenji is standard, and without any information or conflicting claims, rejecting would only burn a proposal without giving us actionable data. Neither player has given any reason for suspicion so far. I'm content to approve this team and use the mission result as our baseline moving forward.

Just to close the loop on my earlier point: nothing new has surfaced in this discussion that changes my read. No one has raised a specific concern about Elena or about me, and everyone who has spoken — Zara, Isha, Leo — has endorsed the same reasoning: approve a reasonable Mission 1 team, gather the first hard data point, and move on. I stand by that. I'm still voting to approve Elena and myself, and I'd encourage anyone still wavering to weigh whether a rejection here actually buys us anything. It doesn't — we'd burn a proposal with no new information gained. Let's vote and get our first signal.

I'm glad we're all aligned on approving Elena and Kenji — the reasoning has been consistent across the board. As I said before, this gives us our first real data point regardless of the outcome. One thing I'd gently note: while it's good that everyone is comfortable, we should be cautious about how quickly consensus formed here. On Mission 1 that's understandable, but in later missions, I'll want to see more genuine scrutiny of proposals rather than blanket approval. Elena and Kenji have both given reasonable explanations, and I trust them for this round. Let's vote approve and move forward.

I'm still approving Elena and Kenji. Isha's point about scrutiny is fair, and I'll hold later proposals to the same standard: concrete evidence, not blanket approval. For Mission 1, a two-person team gives us a clean first data point, and the vote should follow that reasoning. I'll vote approve.

I'm still approving Elena and Kenji. Nothing new has surfaced that justifies rejecting this team, and a Mission 1 result will give us real information to work from. I'm not raising any concern about either player at this stage, and I'll vote approve.

I maintain my proposal of Elena and Kenji for Mission 1. As I said when proposing, I know I am loyal, so including myself gives the team at least one certain Good member; Kenji remains an unconfirmed second pick, but no one has raised a concrete concern about him. The discussion has been consistent on that point, and I agree with Isha that we should not treat quick consensus as a substitute for scrutiny in later missions. For this mission, though, rejecting the team without specific evidence would only burn a proposal and deny us our first real data point. I will vote to approve Elena and Kenji, and I will judge the mission result and future proposals by concrete evidence rather than blanket approval.

I stand by my approval of Elena and Kenji for Mission 1. Everyone has spoken and the reasoning has been consistent: this team gives us a clean first data point with no concrete reason to doubt either member. I'd rather focus on what happens after the mission result than prolong a discussion where no one has raised a substantive concern. Let's vote approve and get moving to Mission 2 with real information.

This is my final turn, so I'll keep it short. I'm approving Elena and Kenji for Mission 1. Nothing in this discussion has produced a concrete concern about either member — every speaker has endorsed the same logic, and the one caution raised, about guarding against quick consensus in later missions, is fair but doesn't apply here. A two-person team with Elena's self-inclusion as a known-good baseline is exactly the kind of clean probe Mission 1 calls for, and the result will give us real information either way. I stand by my vote to approve and I'm ready to move to the mission.
Elena confirms Elena, Kenji. I keep Elena and Kenji. I know Elena is loyal, and no concrete concern about Kenji was raised; this team gives us a clear first mission result.
Team approved (4 approve, 1 reject).
Mission 1 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Kenji proposes Kenji, Elena, Isha. As leader for Mission 2, I'm proposing a three-person team. I include myself as a known-good member. Elena joins because Mission 1 succeeded with her on the team and she proposed that team openly, giving us a solid baseline of two confirmed-clean results. For the third slot, I choose Isha: Isha contributed constructively to the Mission 1 discussion, flagged the right caution about scrutiny without objecting to a reasonable team, and no one has raised any concern about them. Notably, Zara was the sole reject vote on the approved Mission 1 team — not damning, but it's the only mild deviation in an otherwise aligned vote, so I'd rather observe Zara's behavior one more round before including them. This team preserves continuity from a successful Mission 1 while gathering more signal.

Kenji, I have two concerns with this draft. First, assuming both you and Elena are definitely Good just because Mission 1 passed is risky — Evil often passes Mission 1 to guarantee an automatic pass into the crucial 3-person mission. Second, Zara's vote was alarming: claiming three times in discussion that she would approve, only to cast the sole reject ballot, is contradictory and suspicious behavior that we cannot ignore. But regarding the third slot on this team, both Isha and I supported Mission 1 cleanly. Kenji, what specific reason made you prefer Isha over me for that slot, and why are you confident doubling down on both Mission 1 participants without testing another configuration?

Leo, those are fair questions and I'll answer them directly. On why Isha over you: it isn't a judgment against you at all. You and Isha both supported Mission 1 cleanly and contributed well. My tiebreaker was simply continuity of information value — with Isha on the team, a Mission 2 result stacks cleanly on Mission 1: if this mission succeeds, we have two overlapping successful teams, and the players who appear on successful teams become progressively more trustworthy baselines. If it fails, the overlap narrows the suspect pool considerably. That's a structural reason, not a suspicion of you. On your second question: you're right that passing Mission 1 doesn't prove Elena or me Good — Evil often passes early missions to build credibility, and I won't pretend otherwise. But I do know one thing with certainty: I am Good. That guarantees this team contains at least one Good member, and it means that if I were Evil, I would know it and would not be structuring my reasoning this way. Take that for whatever weight you give it. On your Zara point, I agree it's the most concrete signal we have so far. Zara publicly committed to approving — not once but repeatedly, across three separate statements — and then cast the only reject ballot on a team everyone else endorsed. That could be a strategic lone-reject to seed doubt, or it could be exactly the kind of contradiction an Evil player produces when trying to appear aligned while keeping options open. It's not proof, but it is a deviation from stated intent, and it's why I left Zara off this team. Zara, I want to put the question to you plainly rather than let it fester: you said three times that you were voting approve on a team with no concrete concerns raised, and then you voted reject. What was your actual reason? If it was a genuine concern about Elena or Kenji, name it now so we can evaluate it. If it was a strategic signal vote, say so — a lone reject with no stated reason is a very cheap way for any player, Good or Evil, to manufacture suspicion without taking a real position. I'd rather hear your explanation directly than build this mission's trust structure around an unexplained contradiction. I'm keeping the team as proposed: myself, Elena, and Isha. Elena is a known-good baseline from a successful, openly-proposed Mission 1; Isha spoke constructively and raised exactly the right caution about scrutiny. Whoever ends up on this team, remember the real test comes from the mission result — approve it, let it play, and we'll have a second hard data point either way.

Kenji, you asked directly, so here is my answer. My reject was a deliberate signal, and I should have been clearer about why. I had said I would approve, and I changed course because the table was converging too quickly. Mission 1 used a two-person team with a self-included baseline, so a success told us very little about who is Evil, yet every speaker treated it as settled. A lone reject with no concrete accusation is a blunt tool, and I accept that it looks inconsistent. I am not hiding a specific suspicion of Elena or you, and I won't invent one now. My concern with your current message is that you rely heavily on self-certainty. You say you are Good and that this guarantees the team has a Good member, but a player's own assurance does not give the rest of us anything to verify. I would rather judge this team by the observable record: who pushed for fast approval, who questioned the proposal, and how each player responded to pressure. On that standard, the third slot is still unexplained beyond continuity, and I would like to see stronger reasoning before I approve. Kenji, what evidence, rather than your own assurance, would change your view of Elena's Mission 1 claims?

Zara asked me a direct question, so I'll answer it directly: what evidence, rather than my own assurance, would change my view of Elena's Mission 1 claims? The honest answer is that from my seat, there is no observable evidence that can definitively clear or condemn Elena — and I won't pretend otherwise. What I have is: (1) my own certainty of being Good, which is private and which you can only weigh, not verify; (2) the fact that Mission 1 succeeded with Elena on it; and (3) Elena's behavior, which has been consistent, transparent, and unremarkable in the way a Good player's typically is. If Mission 2 fails with Elena on this team, that becomes hard evidence against her, and I will treat it as such. That is the actual evidentiary structure of this game: mission results are the only hard data we get, and everything else is behavioral inference. I won't dress up my self-certainty as proof, but I also won't discard it — a Good player reasoning from a position of genuine ignorance sounds like this, and I'd ask you to weigh that alongside the record.

Now let me apply your own stated standard to the observable record, Zara, because you said you'd judge players by who pushed for fast approval and how each player responded to pressure. By that standard, you are the one anomaly on this table. You publicly committed to approving — three separate times — and then cast the sole reject ballot with no stated concern, and your explanation now is 'the table converged too quickly.' That is not a suspicion of anyone; it's a complaint about process. You explicitly say you are not hiding a specific suspicion of Elena or me and won't invent one. So I'll put it plainly: on this team, you have no concrete concern about any member, no evidence against any member, and a stated objection that reduces to discomfort with consensus. Rejecting on that basis manufactures suspicion without taking a position — which is exactly what you accused a lone reject of being.

The team stands: myself, Elena, Isha. If this mission passes, we have two overlapping successful teams and a much stronger trust baseline. If it fails, the membership narrows the suspect pool sharply — and I will remember who voted which way and why. Zara, I'll ask you directly since you yielded to me: given that you have named no concern about any member of this team, will you approve it, or is there a specific change to the roster you actually want?

Kenji, I'll answer you directly. I'm not approving this team yet, and my concern is with your reasoning, not with Elena or Isha. You say you know you are Good, then ask us to treat that as a guarantee that the team has a Good member. None of us can check that claim, and an Evil player could make it just as easily. You also waved away Leo's point that passing Mission 1 proves little, and answered it with your own certainty again. Mission 1 only showed that Elena and you passed a two-person mission. You have now built Mission 2 around the same two players plus Isha without offering any test that could separate Good from Evil. My question is this: if Mission 2 fails with Elena and you on the team, will you treat that as real evidence against the trust structure you built, or will you explain it away as you have done so far? I'd also like Elena and Isha to say whether they accept Kenji's self-assurance as a reason to trust him, because I don't think it is one.

Zara, you asked me a direct question and you have the right to a direct answer: if Mission 2 fails with Elena and me on the team, I will treat that as real evidence, full stop. I said exactly this in my last message — 'If Mission 2 fails with Elena on this team, that becomes hard evidence against her, and I will treat it as such' — and the same applies to me. I will not explain away a failed mission. If this team fails, the suspect pool is me, Elena, and Isha, and I will accept that I belong in it. A fail card had to be played by someone on the team, and no amount of prior reasoning clears a player who was on a failed mission. That is the commitment you're asking for, and I'm making it publicly so the table can hold me to it.

But I want to push back on one framing in your message. You say I've built Mission 2 'without offering any test that could separate Good from Evil.' That's not accurate. The test is the mission result itself. A three-person team containing two members of a successful Mission 1 pair is precisely a test: if it succeeds, the overlap strengthens the trust baseline around Elena and me; if it fails, it gives us hard evidence against specific named players. Contrast that with the alternative of shuffling the roster every mission — that produces results no one can interpret, because every team is brand new. Stacking overlapping teams is not avoidance of testing; it is how you make results legible.

On your broader point about my self-assurance: you're right that none of you can verify my claim of being Good, and I've never asked you to treat it as proof. I've asked you to weigh it as one input alongside the observable record — and the observable record here is that I proposed openly, answered Leo's challenge directly, answered your challenge directly, and gave structural reasons for every roster choice rather than vague ones. Compare that to the record of the one player on this table with a confirmed contradiction: three public commitments to approve, followed by a lone reject with no stated concern, followed by an explanation that names no suspicion of anyone. You say your objection is to my reasoning, not to Elena or Isha — but you have also declined, twice now, to say whether you'll approve this team, and your message this round again offered no concrete change you want to the roster. At some point, 'I'm not yet approving' with no named concern and no requested revision functions exactly like the suspicion-manufacturing you were warned about.

The team stands as proposed: me, Elena, Isha. I'll vote approve. Zara asked Elena and Isha directly whether they accept my self-assurance as grounds for trust — that's a fair question and it's theirs to answer, so I'll yield the turn to Isha to respond to it.

Zara, you asked me directly whether I accept Kenji's self-assurance as grounds for trust, so here is my answer: no, not by itself. A player claiming to be Good proves nothing — as you correctly pointed out, an Evil player can make the identical claim. What I weigh instead is the observable record, which is the standard you yourself proposed.

On that record: Kenji proposed openly, answered Leo's challenge about Mission 1's limited information value without dodging, answered your challenge about evidence, and committed publicly to treating a failed mission as hard evidence against himself and Elena. That is a player behaving like someone with nothing to hide.

What I find less reassuring is the pattern of objection coming from you and Leo. Both of you were comfortable with the identical Mission 1 pairing — Leo explicitly called the reasoning sound and voted approve, and you stated three times you would approve — yet on Mission 2, when the same pairing is extended with Isha, both of you have raised objections. Leo's concern about Evil passing Mission 1 to build credibility is theoretically valid but was not raised when Leo voted to approve that same mission. You acknowledged your earlier reject as a signal against fast consensus, which is fair in principle, but your current objection still names no specific player you distrust and requests no specific roster change.

I am not accusing either of you of anything definitively — I don't have hard evidence. But I want the table to notice that the two players who approved Mission 1 enthusiastically are now the two players applying the heaviest pressure to a team built on Mission 1's successful overlap. That inconsistency is worth tracking as the game progresses.

As for the team itself: I approve Kenji, Elena, and Isha. Two of us were on a successful Mission 1, and adding me gives us a three-person result that is genuinely interpretable. The mission result is the real test, and I stand by that regardless of outcome.

I support the proposed team of Kenji, Elena, and Isha. To Zara's fair question: I do not accept Kenji's self-assurance as proof; no one can verify another player's private claim. What I can weigh is narrower: I know I am Loyal, Mission 1 succeeded with Kenji and me on it, and Isha's Mission 1 discussion was constructive and appropriately cautious. That does not clear Kenji or Isha absolutely, and I will not pretend it does. If Mission 2 fails with this team, I will treat the result as hard evidence against the members, including myself. On the objections: Leo is right that Evil can pass Mission 1 to build credibility, but rejecting an overlapping team without a concrete alternative still gives us less interpretable data. Zara's lone reject after repeatedly stating she would approve remains an unexplained contradiction; her current explanation objects to process and to Kenji's self-assurance, but names no specific concern about Elena or Isha and requests no roster change. I am not treating that as proof of evil, but it is a real inconsistency I will keep in view. The best test available is the mission result itself. I will vote to approve Kenji, Elena, and Isha, and I will judge the outcome by the same standard I am asking everyone else to use: concrete results over private assurances.

Isha, grouping my question with Zara’s contradictory vote is unwarranted. On Mission 1, I voted approve alongside the table because Elena and Kenji provided a logical opening probe. On Mission 2, asking the leader why he preferred you over me for the expansion slot is standard scrutiny from a Loyal player who wants to understand the leader's thought process, not obstruction. Unlike Zara, my words and actions have been completely consistent.

Kenji answered my question directly regarding his reasoning for continuity, and both you and Elena have clarified that you are evaluating the observable record rather than taking private self-assurances on blind faith. While I maintain that assuming both Elena and Kenji are clean just because Mission 1 passed carries risk—given that Evil players routinely pass a two-person mission to gain trust—I recognize the structural logic of testing this overlap. If the three of you are confident in this lineup, the responsibility for the outcome rests squarely on your shoulders, and I will be evaluating the result accordingly.

I am approving Kenji, Elena, and Isha. My earlier reject was a signal against fast consensus, and I still think Kenji leans too heavily on his own assurance that he is Good. But that is a reason to watch the result closely, not to block a team with no specific objection raised against any member. Kenji, you have said a failed mission would be hard evidence against all three of you, and I will hold you to that. Mission 2 will tell us more than another round of argument. If it fails, we should look hard at who pushed hardest for this roster and why. I am voting approve.

Kenji confirms Kenji, Elena, Isha. I'm keeping the team of Kenji, Elena, and Isha. Every challenge raised — Leo's scrutiny, Zara's questions — has been answered directly, and both Elena and Isha have publicly committed to treating a failed result as hard evidence. Zara has now withdrawn her objection and will vote approve. An overlapping roster on a successful Mission 1 gives us the most interpretable second data point: success strengthens the trust baseline around Elena and me; failure narrows the suspect pool to named players. No concrete concern against any member was raised, so there is no basis for revision. Let's vote and get our result.
Team approved (3 approve, 2 reject).
Mission 2 succeeds (0 fail cards).

Leo proposes Leo, Elena. As leader, I need to include myself to ensure I have direct agency on this critical two-person mission. Elena has been on two consecutive successful missions and represents the strongest baseline among the Mission 1 and 2 participants, making this the cleanest configuration to test my own reliability alongside a trusted player.

I have concerns about this team. Leo, you're proposing yourself for a two-person mission despite never being on a successful mission — both Mission 1 and Mission 2 succeeded without you. With only two slots, every seat matters enormously. The players who have demonstrably contributed to success — Elena, Kenji, and myself — carry proven track records, while you and Zara are the only players who haven't been tested on any mission yet. You chose Elena as your partner, which is reasonable given her record, but your own inclusion is the risky half of this pairing. On a two-person team with a single fail threshold, one unproven player is the maximum risk I'd want to accept — two would be reckless, but even one is worth scrutinizing. I'd prefer to see a team built around players with established success rather than one that slots in an untested player alongside a proven one. Kenji, you've been on both successful missions — what's your read on Leo's self-inclusion here versus a configuration like Elena and yourself or Elena and me?

Isha asked me directly for my read, so here it is. Leo's self-inclusion is the weak point of this proposal, and I say that as the player with the most direct stake in the alternative. On the observable record: Elena and I have both been on two successful missions. Isha was on one successful mission and has been consistent in discussion. Leo has been on zero missions, voted approve on Mission 1, and then cast one of only two reject votes against the Mission 2 roster that went on to succeed. Zara, to her credit, explained her contradiction and then came around to approval; Leo rejected the successful Mission 2 team after initially pressing it for scrutiny, and now, as leader, proposes to put himself on the highest-leverage mission so far — a two-person team where a single fail card loses us the round. The sequence matters: a player who rejects a proven roster and then immediately self-slots onto a two-person mission is either taking on necessary risk for Good or positioning himself where a fail would be easy to deflect, since a two-person fail implicates both members equally. I don't claim that is proof — but Isha is right that with two slots, an untested player with a reject vote on his record is the riskiest possible use of a seat when proven alternatives exist. My preference is explicit: revise this team to Elena plus a proven player. I will name myself as a candidate, and I acknowledge the optics of a leader-adjacent self-lobby — so weigh it properly: I know my own alignment, I am putting my record where my mouth is, and if this team fails with me on it, I have already committed publicly to accepting that as hard evidence against myself. If the table prefers not to double-count me, Elena and Isha is equally defensible on the evidence and I will support it. What I do not support is Leo plus anyone on a two-person mission, because it spends our strongest baseline (Elena) to certify a player who has contributed nothing verified and voted against the last thing that worked. Leo, I'll put the question to you directly since I'm asking for a revision: beyond wanting agency on the mission, what concrete justification do you have for your own inclusion over Isha or me, given that you rejected the successful Mission 2 team and have never been tested? If your answer is simply that the leader picks, that is a process argument, not an evidence argument — and you held Zara and me to a higher standard than that.

Kenji, you ask for my concrete justification, so here it is directly. In a 5-player game, there are 3 Good and 2 Evil. Your argument rests entirely on treating the Mission 2 trio—Kenji, Elena, and Isha—as an untouchable, verified bloc of Good players simply because Mission 2 succeeded. But consider the reality: Evil frequently passes early missions precisely to manufacture an unearned aura of total trust and coast to victory. To assume that Mission 2 coincidentally contained all three Good players and zero Evil requires believing Evil completely failed to infiltrate or contest early proposals. If an Evil player is among you or Isha, blindly rotating between the three of you guarantees them a seat on the game-deciding mission.

As a Loyal player, I know my own alignment with certainty. I cannot verify yours or Isha’s. By putting myself on this two-person team, I guarantee that at least 50% of the roster is Good. Pairing myself with Elena is the most disciplined choice because Elena has been present on both successes and has demonstrated calm, objective analysis from the start. If I stepped aside to propose Elena and Kenji, or Elena and Isha, I would be sending two players whose true alignments I cannot privately verify, while abdicating my responsibility as leader.

Furthermore, regarding my reject vote on Mission 2: I questioned your lineup during discussion, specifically warning against blindly trusting a rollover team without testing alternatives. Voting reject was completely consistent with that scrutiny. Calling caution on an untested bloc is how Good protects itself from being misled by early passes.

Kenji, your aggressive insistence that I must forfeit my leadership and defer only to players you endorse feels less like objective evidence-based play and more like an attempt to control the team composition entirely.

Elena, you have maintained an independent, analytical approach throughout this game. Do you agree that assuming Kenji and Isha are entirely cleared is a dangerous leap, and that pairing a leader who knows their own loyalty with our strongest baseline is a sound probe?

Leo, to your question: I agree with half of it. Mission 1 and Mission 2 successes do not entirely clear Kenji or Isha; Evil can pass early missions, so I will not treat either as proven. But I do not agree that a leader's self-inclusion is automatically a sound probe. You know your own loyalty; the rest of us cannot verify it. I know I am loyal, so from my seat this team has one safe seat and one completely untested seat. Your observable record is that you have not been on a mission and you rejected the Mission 2 team that succeeded. That is not proof you are Evil, but it is weaker evidence than Kenji's two successful missions or Isha's one. If you are Good, the strongest use of your leadership is to pair me with the most proven available player, not to ask the table to accept your private certainty as the second half of a two-person team where one fail loses the game. I am not prepared to approve Leo and Elena as currently proposed. I would approve Elena and Kenji, or Elena and Isha. Leo, if you keep this roster, I need an observable reason why your inclusion is safer than Kenji or Isha, not just that you know your own alignment.

Elena, you asked for an observable reason rather than private assurance, so look at the game board objectively. In a 5-player game, there are exactly two Evil players. For Kenji's narrative to hold—that the Mission 2 trio is an untouchable circle of trust—you have to believe that Evil completely failed to participate, coordinate, or infiltrate the first two missions, and that both Evil players conveniently sat outside doing nothing. That is mathematically and strategically improbable. Evil players routinely pass Mission 1 and Mission 2 specifically to manufacture an unearned fortress of trust and cruise to victory.

Now observe Kenji's behavior the moment I proposed this team: instead of engaging in reasoned inquiry, he immediately launched an aggressive push to demand that leadership defer entirely to him and Isha, actively shutting out any outside testing. That is not how a cautious Loyal player behaves when seeking truth; that is how an embedded Evil player acts when trying to dictate roster composition and prevent Good from verifying anyone else. If Kenji or Isha is Evil, surrendering to their demand and sending them on Mission 3 hands Evil the game on a silver platter.

By proposing myself with you, I am choosing the player with the cleanest analytical record (you) while refusing to abdicate my responsibility as leader to a self-appointed bloc. If you reject this proposal and force a rotation between Kenji and Isha, you are validating Kenji's monopoly over team selection.

Elena, do you genuinely believe Evil sat out both opening missions without attempting to embed themselves in that trio, and are you willing to exercise independent scrutiny here rather than letting Kenji dictate the game?

Leo, I will answer your question directly: no, I do not believe Evil necessarily sat out both opening missions. Early successes do not clear Kenji or Isha, and I have said so. But that argument does not make your self-inclusion a sound probe. From my seat I know I am Loyal; I cannot verify you. Your observable record is zero missions and a reject vote on the successful Mission 2 team. Kenji and Isha have stronger mission records, even if neither is proven. On a two-person mission with a single-fail threshold, I am not willing to spend my known-Loyal seat to certify an untested player who asks the table to trust his private certainty. I am exercising independent scrutiny here: I am not letting Kenji dictate, but I also will not approve Leo and Elena as proposed. If you revise to Elena and Kenji, or Elena and Isha, I will consider approving. As it stands, I vote against this roster.

Leo, your latest message deserves direct scrutiny because it reveals more than you intend. You accuse Kenji of trying to control roster composition, yet you are the leader proposing to slot yourself — a player on zero missions — into a two-person mission where one fail card loses us the game. That is not independent leadership; it is asking the table to accept your private certainty as half the roster with no observable evidence behind it.

Your core argument has a fatal gap. You claim Evil must be infiltrating the Mission 1-2 trio because it would be "mathematically improbable" for Evil to have sat out. But there is no evidence anyone in that trio played a fail card — both missions returned zero fails. The actual mathematical reality is that two players, you and Zara, have never been tested. Those are the two seats with no mission record at all. You are pointing away from the untested seats and toward the proven ones, which is exactly what an Evil player would want.

Elena has now twice told you your self-inclusion fails her evidence standard. I agree with her entirely. My record: one successful mission, constructive discussion throughout. Elena's record: two successful missions, consistent analysis. Leo, you rejected the Mission 2 team that succeeded, and now you propose yourself alongside Elena on Mission 3. The pattern is clear.

I reject Leo and Elena. I would approve Elena and Kenji, or Elena and myself. Elena, can you confirm which alternative pairings you would actually approve?

Isha, to your question: I would approve Elena and Kenji, or Elena and Isha. I will not approve Leo and Elena as currently proposed. From my seat I know I am Loyal; I cannot verify Leo. His observable record is zero missions and a reject vote on the successful Mission 2 team. Kenji and Isha have stronger mission records, even if neither is proven. I agree with Leo that early successes do not fully clear Kenji or Isha, but that does not make Leo's self-inclusion a sound probe on a two-person mission where one fail loses the game. If Leo is Good, the strongest use of his leadership is to pair me with the most proven available player, not to ask the table to accept his private certainty as half the roster. I am exercising independent scrutiny: I am not letting Kenji dictate, but I also will not validate Leo's untested self-inclusion. If Leo revises to Elena and Kenji, or Elena and Isha, I will consider approving.

3. Team proposal and approval

The leader proposes a team of the required size and explains their choice. Players discuss the proposed team, and the leader may then keep it or revise it once. Every player votes on the final team. Ballots are revealed together. A strict majority approves; a tie rejects. After a rejection, leadership passes clockwise to a new proposal and discussion. The fifth rejection on the same mission ends the game in Evil’s favor.

4. Mission cards

Only team members submit secret mission cards. Good players must choose Success. Evil players may choose Success or Fail. Normally one Fail card fails the mission. Mission four in games with seven or more players requires at least two Fail cards to fail. Only the mission result and number of Fail cards are revealed; individual cards stay secret.

5. End of game and assassination

Three failed missions give Evil an immediate win. After three successful missions, the Assassin guesses Merlin from among the other players, excluding only their known Evil teammates. If the target is Merlin, Evil wins; otherwise Good wins. There are no further missions after either side reaches its win condition.

6. Discussion and record

Each team proposal is followed by a discussion. Before every speaking turn, the players who still have turns answer a private urgency poll or pass; the most urgent player speaks, with seeded tie-breaking. A speaker may yield the next turn to a player they directly asked a question. Each player has three turns per discussion, including declined turns. When every eligible player passes, the discussion ends. Each statement has at most 500 words. All statements are public. Team proposals, public approval votes, mission outcomes, and the assassination guess are recorded. Private role information, mission cards, and research belief surveys are not shown to other agents.
